claim: Prior experience accelerates acquisition of novel, related information through processes like assimilation into mental schemas.
source: Prior experience accelerates acquisition of novel, related information through processes like assimilation into mental schemas, but the underlying neuronal mechanisms are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle being investigated.

claim: Specific representations of de novo experiences on linear environments were formed on a framework of pre-configured network activity expressed in the preceding sleep.
source: We found that specific representations of de novo experiences on linear environments were formed on a framework of pre configured network activity expressed in the preceding sleep and were rapidly, flexibly adjusted via NMDAR-dependent activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: De novo spatial representations were rapidly and flexibly adjusted via NMDAR-dependent activity.
source: We found that specific representations of de novo experiences on linear environments were formed on a framework of pre configured network activity expressed in the preceding sleep and were rapidly, flexibly adjusted via NMDAR-dependent activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing CT and KO mice.

claim: Prior experience accelerated encoding of subsequent experiences on contiguous or isolated novel tracks, significantly decreasing their NMDAR-dependence.
source: This prior experience accelerated encoding of subsequent experiences on contiguous or isolated novel tracks, significantly decreasing their NMDAR-dependence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data from contiguous and disjunct conditions.

claim: De novo learning of an alternation task was facilitated by CA3 NMDARs.
source: Similarly, de novo learning of an alternation task was facilitated by CA3 NMDARs; this experience accelerated subsequent learning of related tasks, independent of CA3 NMDARs, consistent with a schema-based learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6.

claim: Prior experience on an alternation task accelerated subsequent learning of related tasks, independent of CA3 NMDARs, consistent with schema-based learning.
source: Similarly, de novo learning of an alternation task was facilitated by CA3 NMDARs; this experience accelerated subsequent learning of related tasks, independent of CA3 NMDARs, consistent with a schema-based learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6.

claim: Hippocampal dysfunction results in anterograde amnesia while sparing recollection of old, schema-based memories.
source: These results reveal the existence of distinct neuronal encoding schemes which could explain why hippocampal dysfunction results in anterograde amnesia while sparing recollection of old, schema-based memories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results stated in the abstract, drawing on established knowledge about hippocampal function.

claim: Individual hippocampal neurons fire at specific spatial locations of the animal during free exploration of spatial environments (place cells).
source: During the free exploration of spatial environments, individual hippocampal neurons fire at specific spatial locations of the animal and are activated sequentially along the trajectory of the animal (place cells) (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; McNaughton et al., 1983; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Lee and Wilson, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sequences of place cells with partially overlapping fields fire with compressed temporal delays that correspond to the Euclidian distance between the location of their place field peaks.
source: Sequences of place cells with partially overlapping fields fire with compressed temporal delays that correspond to the Euclidian distance between the location of their place field peaks (Muller et al., 1996; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sequence compression is thought to be an animal model of the internal representation of an external space by place cell assemblies in the CA1 area of the rodent hippocampus.
source: This phenomenon, known as sequence compression (Skaggs et al., 1996; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006) is thought to be an animal model of the internal representation of an external space by the place cell assemblies in the CA1 area of the rodent hippocampus (Skaggs et al., 1996; Dragoi et al., 2003; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: The upstream auto-associative area CA3 has been proposed to orchestrate the functional organization of cellular assemblies in the downstream CA1 region.
source: The upstream auto-associative area, CA3, has been proposed to orchestrate (Tsodyks, 1999; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006), together with entorhinal cortex and via synaptic plasticity (Dragoi et al., 2003), the functional organization of cellular assemblies (Hebb, 1949; McNaughton et al., 1996; Harris et al., 2003; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006) in the downstream CA1 region, the source of the hippocampal output to the rest of the cortex.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: According to a prevailing model, novel temporal and spatial place cell sequences emerge rapidly in the hippocampus upon exploration of a novel linear track predominantly or exclusively in response to complex stimuli from the external environment with minimal or no contribution from internal neuronal dynamics.
source: According to a prevailing model, novel temporal and spatial place cell sequences emerge rapidly in the hippocampus upon exploration of a novel linear track predominantly or exclusively in response to the complex stimuli from the external environment and with minimal or no contribution from the internal neuronal dynamics around the time of the exploration (Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Lee and Wilson, 2002).
evidence: This describes a prevailing model from the literature that the current study challenges.

claim: Place cell sequences are replayed during periods of resting or sleep at higher incidences and perhaps facilitate the consolidation of the encoded information.
source: Subsequently, these sequences are replayed during periods of resting (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsaki, 2007; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011) or sleep (Nadasdy et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009) at higher incidences and perhaps facilitate the consolidation of the encoded information (Girardeau et al., 2009; Nakashiba et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Jadhav et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature, with speculation about consolidation function.

claim: Temporal sequences of firing that correlated with place cell sequences formed during exploration of a novel linear track had been expressed during the resting/sleep period preceding the exploration (preplay).
source: Recently, we described that temporal sequences of firing that correlated with place cell sequences formed during the exploration of a novel linear track had been expressed during the resting/sleep period preceding the exploration, a phenomenon called preplay (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013).
evidence: This refers to prior work by the authors.

claim: Spontaneous neuronal activity preceding a novel spatial experience may prime and contribute to the formation of new spatial representations via a neuronal ensemble selection process.
source: We proposed that spontaneous neuronal activity preceding a novel spatial experience may prime and contribute to the formation of new spatial representations via a neuronal ensemble selection process (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their prior work.

claim: CA3 NMDAR KO mice had their CA3 NR1 subunit knocked-out using a Cre/loxP recombination system.
source: These mutant mice had their CA3 NR1 subunit knocked-out using a Cre/loxP recombination system (Tsien et al., 1996; Nakazawa et al., 2002) and are referred to as the CA3 NMDAR KO, or simply KO mice.
evidence: This describes the genetic manipulation used in the study.

claim: Deletion of the NR1 subunit in the CA3 area abolished the NMDAR currents in the CA3 pyramidal cells, but not in the downstream CA1 and upstream dentate gyrus area neurons.
source: Previous studies using these two groups of mice have shown that deletion of the NR1 subunit in the CA3 area abolished the NMDAR currents in the CA3 pyramidal cells, but not in the downstream CA1 and upstream dentate gyrus area neurons (Nakazawa et al., 2002), which resulted in impaired memory acquisition of one-time experiences (Nakazawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies using the same mouse model.

claim: Deletion of the NR1 subunit in the CA3 area resulted in impaired memory acquisition of one-time experiences.
source: Previous studies using these two groups of mice have shown that deletion of the NR1 subunit in the CA3 area abolished the NMDAR currents in the CA3 pyramidal cells, but not in the downstream CA1 and upstream dentate gyrus area neurons (Nakazawa et al., 2002), which resulted in impaired memory acquisition of one-time experiences (Nakazawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies using the same mouse model.

claim: The lack of post-synaptic NMDAR function blocks the induction of long-term potentiation of synaptic transmission in the hippocampus.
source: The lack of post-synaptic NMDAR function has been shown to block the induction of long-term potentiation of synaptic transmission in the hippocampus (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Tsien et al., 1996) and other brain areas, a mechanism proposed to underlie learning and memory (Morris et al., 1986; Tsien et al., 1996; Moser et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Long-term potentiation is a mechanism proposed to underlie learning and memory.
source: The lack of post-synaptic NMDAR function has been shown to block the induction of long-term potentiation of synaptic transmission in the hippocampus (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Tsien et al., 1996) and other brain areas, a mechanism proposed to underlie learning and memory (Morris et al., 1986; Tsien et al., 1996; Moser et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The stability of place cell firing within the run session on novel tracks increased with experience in the de novo condition similarly in CT and KO mice.
source: The stability of place cell firing within the run session on novel tracks increased with experience in the de novo condition similarly in the CT and KO mice (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The stability of place cell firing appeared high from the beginning of the contiguous condition in both CT and KO genotypes.
source: appeared high from the beginning of the contiguous condition in both genotypes (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The stability of place cell firing appeared high from beginning in CT mice and increased with repeated experience in KO mice in the disjunct condition.
source: and appeared high from beginning in the CT mice and increased with repeated experience in KO mice in the disjunct condition (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The spatial tuning of CA1 place cells was relatively poor in session 1 (DnRun1) in both CT and KO mice by the measure of place field length.
source: Under the de novo condition, the spatial tuning of CA1 place cells was relatively poor in session 1 (DnRun1) in both CT (Cacucci et al., 2007) and KO mice (Nakazawa et al., 2003) by the measure of place field length (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and consistent with cited literature.

claim: Spatial tuning increased faster in CT vs KO mice from session 1 to session 2 in the de novo condition.
source: Spatial tuning increased faster in CT vs KO mice from session 1 to session 2 (Figure 2A, left and 2B left, paired difference in place field length DnRun1–DnRun2, 8 ± 2.3 cm, p<0.003, paired t test in CT; 0.6 ± 2.4 cm, p=0.78 in KO; CT vs KO, p<0.027, ranksum test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Spatial tuning increased within-session DnRun1 in CT but not KO mice.
source: and within-session DnRun1 (Figure 2C, left, spatial tuning, 4.8 ± 2.1 cm, p<0.003 in CT; −0.7 ± 1.5 cm, p=0.3 in KO; CT vs KO, p<0.015, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: An overnight holding in the home cage led to significantly increased spatial tuning in KO mice the next day.
source: An overnight holding in the home cage led to significantly increased spatial tuning in KO mice the next day (Figure 2A, DnRun1 compared to FamRun1, 29.6 ± 2.6 cm compared to 20.6 ± 2.0 cm, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The average number of place fields per place cell (>1 Hz) was not different across genotypes and experimental sessions.
source: The average number of place fields per place cell (>1 Hz) was not different across genotypes and experimental sessions (CT vs KO: 1.52 vs 1.58 fields/place cell in DnRun1, p>0.5, ranksum test; 1.50 vs 1.53 in DnRun2, p>0.7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The experience- and genotype-dependent changes in place field size result from the spatial tuning of initially large place fields rather than from the scattering of large place fields into multiple smaller ones.
source: This result indicates that the experience- and genotype-dependent changes in place field size reported above (Figure 2B–C) result from the spatial tuning of initially large place fields rather than from the scattering of large place fields into multiple smaller ones.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on place field numbers.

claim: There was a significant increase in the lap-by-lap correlations with increased experience for both genotypes, although the increase occurred faster in CT compared to KO mice.
source: At the neuronal ensemble level, there was a significant increase in the lap-by-lap correlations with increased experience for both genotypes, although the increase occurred faster in CT compared to KO mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In CT but not KO mice, the increase in lap-by-lap correlations reached a plateau by the second exploratory session (DnRun2) under the de novo condition.
source: In the CT, but not KO mice, the increase reached a plateau by the second exploratory session (DnRun2) under the de novo condition (Figure 2D, DnRun1 compared to DnRun2, 0.37 ± 0.007 compared to 0.48 ± 0.01, p<10−13, ranksum test in CT mice; 0.38 ± 0.005 compared to 0.38 ± 0.004, p=0.38 in KO mice; CT vs KO in DnRun2, p<10−9, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The correlations eventually reached stable CT levels in KO mice by the next day.
source: Although the correlations eventually reached stable CT levels in KO mice, this did not occur until the next day (Figure 2D, DnRun1 compared to Fam, 0.37 ± 0.007 compared to 0.48 ± 0.01, p<10−13 in CT and 0.38 ± 0.005 compared to 0.48 ± 0.01 in KO, p<10−10).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The first-time spatial experience on a linear track leads to a gradual increase in spatial tuning and co-variation of ensembles of CA1 place cells encoding the novel experience.
source: These results suggest that the first-time spatial experience on a linear track leads to a gradual increase in spatial tuning and co-variation of ensembles of CA1 place cells encoding the novel experience, and that the temporal dynamics of these processes are facilitated by NMDAR-dependent activity in the auto-associative area CA3 of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from the de novo condition.

claim: The temporal dynamics of spatial tuning and co-variation processes are facilitated by NMDAR-dependent activity in the auto-associative area CA3 of the hippocampus.
source: These results suggest that the first-time spatial experience on a linear track leads to a gradual increase in spatial tuning and co-variation of ensembles of CA1 place cells encoding the novel experience, and that the temporal dynamics of these processes are facilitated by NMDAR-dependent activity in the auto-associative area CA3 of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results comparing CT and KO mice.

claim: CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity and plasticity are specifically involved in the rapid within-session changes in single and ensemble place cell activity.
source: The results suggest that CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity and plasticity are specifically involved in the rapid within-session changes in single and ensemble place cell activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results showing differences between CT and KO mice in within-session dynamics.

claim: For both genotypes, the new place fields were as spatially tuned during the first session (ContigRun) in the novel arm of the L-shaped track as in the contiguous familiar arm.
source: Surprisingly, for both genotypes, the new place fields were as spatially tuned during the first session (ContigRun) in the novel arm of the L-shaped track as in the contiguous familiar arm (Figure 2A,E) and as in the preceding FamRun1 session (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and 2E.

claim: No additional spatial tuning could be detected within the ContigRun session within each group of mice.
source: No additional spatial tuning could be detected within the ContigRun session within each group of mice (Figure 2B–C; FamRun1 compared to ContigRun: 22.1 ± 1.7 cm compared to 23.9 ± 1.7 cm, p=0.46 in CT and 20.6 ± 2.0 cm compared to 21.9 ± 1.1 cm, p=0.34 in KO), across genotypes (CT compared to KO, p=0.6 in FamRun1, p=0.46 in ContigRun), and for both the familiar and the novel portions of the L-shaped track (Figure 2E, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and 2E.

claim: The increased lap-by-lap correlations observed in FamRun1 were preserved in the ContigRun session for both groups of mice.
source: Similarly, the increased lap-by-lap correlations observed in FamRun1 were preserved in the ContigRun session for both groups of mice (Figure 2D,F; FamRun1 compared to ContigRun, 0.48 ± 0.01 compared to 0.47 ± 0.009, p=0.41 in CT and 0.48 ± 0.01 compared to 0.46 ± 0.01, p=0.2 in KO), and there were no significant differences in the correlations between genotypes (CT compared to KO, p=0.98 in FamRun1, p=0.42 in ContigRun), nor between the familiar and the novel portions of the L-shaped track (Figure 2F, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2D and 2F.

claim: Under the contiguous condition, independent of CA3 NMDARs, the spatial information regarding the previously unvisited novel portion of the L-shaped track was rapidly bound with the existing stable representation of the familiar track.
source: These results suggest that under the contiguous condition, independent of CA3 NMDARs, the spatial information regarding the previously unvisited novel portion of the L-shaped track was rapidly bound with the existing stable representation of the familiar track given the animals' prior experience on the familiar track.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from the contiguous condition.

claim: The rapid dynamics on the novel arm during the Contig session may reflect the prior recruitment at a subthreshold firing level of the new place cells into stable, tuned cortico-hippocampal cellular assemblies during pre-exposures to the familiar track.
source: These rapid dynamics on the novel arm during the Contig session are in contrast to the slow dynamics of place field tuning and co-variation during de novo exposure to a novel track (i.e., the DnRun1 session for CT and DnRun1–2 sessions for KO). This may reflect the prior recruitment at a subthreshold firing level of the new place cells (Epsztein et al., 2011) into stable, tuned cortico-hippocampal cellular assemblies during pre-exposures to the familiar track, which manifested as preplay of the novel arm during the preceding sleep or resting epochs (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results, drawing on cited literature.

claim: Exploration of the novel track in the disjunct condition induced a significant, albeit transient, increase in the CA1 place field length in KO but not CT mice.
source: In this case, exploration of the novel track induced a significant, albeit transient, increase in the CA1 place field length in KO but not CT mice (FamRun2 vs DisjRun1: 23.9 ± 1.4 vs 23.9 ± 1.5 cm in CT, p=0.9; 22.6 ± 1.3 vs 28.9 ± 2 in KO, p<0.01, ranksum test; between genotypes, CT vs KO in DisjRun1, p<0.05; DisjRun1 vs DisjRun2 in KO, p<0.04, Figure 2A; paired difference in place field length FamRun2–DisjRun1 CT vs KO, p<0.027, ranksum test, Figure 2B; within-session DisjRun1, CT vs KO, p<10−3, Figure 2C), consistent with an earlier report (Nakazawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and 2C, and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The increased lap-by-lap correlations recorded on the familiar track (FamRun2) decreased with novelty (DisjRun1) in KO but not in CT mice.
source: The increased lap-by-lap correlations recorded on the familiar track (FamRun2) decreased with novelty (DisjRun1) in KO but not in CT mice (FamRun2 vs DisjRun1: 0.49 ± 0.006 vs 0.51 ± 0.008, p>0.05 in CT; 0.47 ± 0.005 vs 0.41 ± 0.004, p<10−15 in KO; DisjRun1: CT vs KO, p<10−30; DisjRun1 vs DisjRun2 in KO, p<10−4, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The correlations returned to 'familiar levels' by the next session (DisjRun2) in the KO mice more rapidly compared to the de novo condition.
source: The correlations returned to 'familiar levels' by the next session (DisjRun2) in the KO mice more rapidly compared to the de novo condition (compare DisjRun2 to DnRun2 in KO, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The dynamics in place field tuning and lap-by-lap correlations were not due to differences in the velocity of animal movement across sessions or genotypes.
source: Overall, these dynamics were not due to differences in the velocity of animal movement across sessions or genotypes (Figure 2G), as place field size and lap-by-lap correlations were not significantly correlated with the animal velocity (p>0.11 and p>0.12, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In CT mice, cells from all three groups of place field distance changes displayed relatively high lap-by-lap co-variation during DisjRun1 exploration.
source: In the CT mice, cells from all three groups displayed relatively high lap-by-lap co-variation during DisjRun1 exploration (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: In KO mice, only cells of the stable assemblies (within 5 cm change) maintained a high lap-by-lap co-variation during DisjRun1, while groups of pairs with changes larger than 5 cm exhibited significantly poorer co-variation.
source: In contrast, in KO mice, only cells of the stable assemblies (within 5 cm change) maintained a high lap-by-lap co-variation during DisjRun1, while groups of pairs with changes larger than 5 cm exhibited significantly poorer co-variation (Figure 2I, p<0.05, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: A certain group of cell pairs (stable assemblies) counters a complete NMDAR-dependent reorganization of the entire neuronal population in response to novel stimuli by maintaining their co-variation independent of CA3 NMDARs.
source: These results suggest a modular, higher order organization of cellular assemblies, in which a certain group of cell pairs (stable assemblies) counters a complete NMDAR-dependent reorganization of the entire neuronal population in response to novel stimuli by maintaining their co-variation independent of CA3 NMDARs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from the disjunct condition.

claim: The changes in cellular ensemble organization upon exploration of the contiguous novel arm are CA3 NMDARs-independent.
source: A similar grouping of the cell pairs active in the contiguous condition during FamRun1 and ContigRun revealed that the changes in cellular ensemble organization upon exploration of the contiguous novel arm are CA3 NMDARs-independent (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The ensemble of place cells formed distinct representations across the two environments, a process called remapping.
source: The large proportion of cell pairs showing >20 cm changes in their spatial relationship from familiar to novel tracks (>65% in CT, >53% in KO mice) indicates that the ensemble of place cells formed distinct representations across the two environments, a process called remapping (Muller and Kubie, 1987; Dragoi et al., 2003; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on place field distance changes, drawing on cited literature.

claim: The order in which the place cells fired in the familiar track was not correlated with their order of firing in the novel arm or novel track.
source: Consistent with the remapping, the order in which the place cells fired in the familiar track (place cell sequences) was not correlated with their order of firing in the novel arm (contiguous condition, mean RCT2 = 0.03, mean RKO2 = 0.12, p>0.05, both genotypes) or novel track (disjunct condition, mean RCT2 = 0.11, mean RKO2 = 0.12, p>0.05, both genotypes)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of sequence correlations.

claim: The order in which place cells fired in the familiar track was similar to the order in which they later fired in the familiar arm of the L-shape track.
source: whereas it was similar to the order in which they later fired in the familiar arm of the L-shape track (contiguous condition, RCT2 = 0.6, RKO2 = 0.5, p<0.05, both genotypes).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of sequence correlations.

claim: For both genotypes and for all experimental conditions and sessions, the absolute correlation values between events occurring during the pre-Run or post-Run sleep/rest session and the original novel track/arm templates were significantly higher than the correlation values obtained using corresponding shuffled templates.
source: For both genotypes and for all experimental conditions and sessions, the absolute correlation values between events occurring during the pre-Run or post-Run sleep/rest session and the original novel track/arm templates (Figure 4A–H) were significantly higher than the correlation values obtained using corresponding shuffled templates (Figure 4, left panels, ranksum test, see 'Materials and methods'; all mice passed individual significance for preplay and replay across conditions, ranksum or binomial probability tests).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4.

claim: With the exception of one CT mouse (CT2), the absolute values of the correlations of the significant events with the spatial templates of the very first run session on the novel track (DnRun1) were similar for the spiking events occurring during the pre-DnRun1 sleep/rest session compared to those occurring during the post-DnRun1 session, both in CT and KO mice.
source: At the level of individual animals, with the exception of one CT mouse (CT2, preplay > replay, p<10−4, ranksum test), the absolute values of the correlations of the significant events with the spatial templates of the very first run session on the novel track (i.e., DnRun1) were similar for the spiking events occurring during the pre-DnRun1 sleep/rest session (i.e., when preplay occurs) compared to those occurring during the post-DnRun1 session (i.e., when replay occurs), both in CT and KO mice (Figure 5Aa, p>0.05, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Aa.

claim: The proportions of significant events out of all events were similar in the pre-DnRun1 vs post-DnRun1 sleep/rest for each individual mouse and genotype.
source: The proportions of significant events out of all events were also similar in the pre-DnRun1 vs post-DnRun1 sleep/rest for each individual mouse and genotype (p>0.05 for each individual animal, Z-test for two proportions, Figure 5Ba; preplay vs replay: 9/132 vs 9/148 in CT1, 237/2255 vs 438/4456 in CT2, 2/10 vs 5/45 in CT3, 7/136 vs 5/71 in CT4, 2/48 vs 4/74 in KO1, 104/1310 vs 112/1496 in KO2, and 80/1146 vs 141/1824 in KO3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Ba.

claim: When the absolute correlation values of the significant events were pulled together from all animals, they were higher for the spiking events occurring during the pre-DnRun1 sleep/rest session (preplay) compared to those occurring during the post-DnRun1 session (replay) in CT but not KO mice.
source: Surprisingly, when the absolute correlation values of the significant events were pulled together from all animals, they were higher for the spiking events occurring during the pre-DnRun1 sleep/rest session (preplay) compared to those occurring during the post-DnRun1 session (replay) in CT but not KO mice (Figure 4A–B, right panels, Figure 5Ca, empty bars; pre-DnRun1 compared to post-DnRun1, 0.87 ± 0.008 (std. 0.12) compared to 0.80 ± 0.007 (std. 0.13), p<10−4 in CT, Figure 4A, right panel, Figure 5Ca, empty bars, left; and 0.89 ± 0.008 (std. 0.1) compared to 0.88 ± 0.007 (std. 0.1), p>0.075 in KO, Figure 4B, right panel, Figure 5Ca, empty bars, right, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 5Ca.

claim: The population of early template correlations was not different from the population of late ones in both CT and KO mice.
source: We found that the population of early template correlations was not different from the population of late ones in both CT and KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both early and late spatial-temporal correlations were higher in the KO mice compared with the CT ones.
source: However, both early and late spatial-temporal correlations were higher in the KO mice compared with the CT ones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relative instability of the place fields during DnRun1 session is associated with a process of relatively mild 'editing' of the early template, rather than with a process of dramatic 'remapping' into a new chart.
source: These results indicate that the relative instability of the place fields during DnRun1 session is associated with a process of relatively mild 'editing' of the early template, rather than with a process of dramatic 'remapping' into a new chart.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results on early vs late template correlations.

claim: Following a second exposure to the novel track, with the exception of one CT mouse (CT2), the significant correlations of spiking events with the DnRun2 templates were similar during post-DnRun2 sleep/rest compared to the pre-DnRun2 sleep/rest in CT and KO mice.
source: Following a second exposure to the novel track, with the exception of one CT mouse (CT2, preplay<replay, p<0.006), the significant correlations of spiking events with the DnRun2 templates were similar during post-DnRun2 sleep/rest compared to the pre-DnRun2 sleep/rest in CT and KO mice (Figure 5Ab, p>0.05, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Ab.

claim: The proportions of significant events were similar before and after the DnRun2 run experience in all mice.
source: Moreover, the proportions of significant events were also similar before and after the DnRun2 run experience in all mice (p>0.05, Z-test for two proportions, Figure 5Bb; proportions preplay vs replay: 15/164 vs 5/69 in CT1, 465/4567 vs 196/1753 in CT2, 21/160 vs 196/1753 in CT3, 3/70 vs 8/131 in CT4, 3/74 vs 8/66 in KO1, 186/1942 vs 261/2578 in KO2, and 223/2504 vs 158/1807 in KO3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Bb.

claim: When absolute correlation values were pulled together across animals, the pre-Run vs post-Run play relationship reversed in the CT but not in the KO animals after the second exposure to the novel track.
source: When absolute correlation values were pulled together across animals, the pre-Run vs post-Run play relationship reversed in the CT but not in the KO animals (Figure 4C–D, right panels, Figure 5Cb, empty bars).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 5Cb.

claim: The significant correlations of spiking events with the DnRun2 templates were stronger during post-DnRun2 sleep/rest compared to the pre-DnRun2 sleep/rest in CT animals.
source: The significant correlations of spiking events with the DnRun2 templates were stronger during post-DnRun2 sleep/rest compared to the pre-DnRun2 sleep/rest in CT animals (pre-DnRun2 compared to post-DnRun2, 0.77 ± 0.006 (std. 0.13) compared to 0.83 ± 0.008 (std. 0.13), p<10−3, ranksum test, Figure 4C, right panel, Figure 5Cb, empty bars, left)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 5Cb.

claim: The significant correlations of spiking events with the DnRun2 templates were similar during post-DnRun2 sleep/rest compared to the pre-DnRun2 sleep/rest in KO mice.
source: however, they were similar in the KO mice (Figure 4D, right panel, Figure 5Cb, empty bars, right; pre-DnRun2 compared to post-DnRun2, 0.85 ± 0.006 (std. 0.11) compared to 0.85 ± 0.006 (std. 0.12), p>0.35).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 5Cb.

claim: In the contiguous condition, both at the individual animal level and at the group level the correlations with the ContigRun templates in the post-ContigRun (replay) were similar to the ones in the pre-ContigRun sleep/rest (preplay) for both genotypes.
source: In the contiguous condition, both at the individual animal level (Figure 5Ac) and at the group level the correlations with the ContigRun templates in the post-ContigRun (i.e., replay) were similar to the ones in the pre-ContigRun sleep/rest (i.e., preplay) for both genotypes (group level; Figure 4E, right panel, Figure 5Cc, empty bars, left, pre-ContigRun compared to post-ContigRun, 0.90 ± 0.01 (std. 0.1) compared to 0.87 ± 0.009 (std. 0.09), p>0.55 in CT mice; Figure 4F, right panel, Figure 5Cc, empty bars, right, pre-ContigRun compared to post-ContigRun, 0.89 ± 0.01 (std. 0.1) vs 0.86 ± 0.007 (std. 0.09), p>0.21 in KO mice, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Ac, Figure 4E-F, and Figure 5Cc.

claim: The proportions of significant events out of all events were similar before and after the ContigRun experience.
source: The proportions of significant events out of all events were also similar before and after the ContigRun experience (Figure 5Bc, p>0.05, Z-test for two proportions; preplay vs replay incidence: 59/1013 vs 83/1601 in CT2, 3/23 vs 21/180 in CT3, 2/51 vs 23/459 in CT4, 28/381 vs 74/903 in KO2, 55/788 vs 114/1422 in KO3, and 7/123 vs 23/418 in KO4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Bc.

claim: In the disjunct condition, at the level of individual animals, the absolute correlation values of significant events and their incidence were similar before and after the DisjRun1 experience.
source: In the disjunct condition, at the level of individual animals, the absolute correlation values of significant events (Figure 5Ad) and their incidence were similar before and after the DisjRun1 experience (Figure 5Bd, p>0.05 for all mice, Z-test for two proportions; preplay vs replay incidence: 541/4822 vs 265/2503 in CT2, 62/824 vs 74/1024 in CT3, 313/2769 vs 164/1410 in CT4, 5/102 vs 3/18 in KO1, 185/1671 vs 33/311 in KO3, and 41/446 vs 103/869 in KO4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Ad and 5Bd.

claim: At the genotype group level, the novel experience (DisjRun1) resulted in slightly increased correlations in the post-DisjRun1 vs pre-DisjRun1 sleep/rest in CT but not KO animals.
source: At the genotype group level, the novel experience (DisjRun1) resulted in slightly increased correlations in the post-DisjRun1 vs pre-DisjRun1 sleep/rest in CT (0.80 ± 0.006 (std. 0.14) vs 0.77 ± 0.005 (std. 0.14), p<0.05, ranksum test, Figure 4G, right panel, Figure 5Cd, empty bars, left), but not KO animals (0.86 ± 0.01 (std. 0.12) vs 0.85 ± 0.009 (std. 0.11), p>0.17, Figure 4H, right panel, Figure 5Cd, empty bars, right).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4G-H and Figure 5Cd.

claim: Across all experimental conditions and sessions and for both genotypes there were no overall changes in the number of cells active per significant event (preplay vs replay).
source: Across all experimental conditions and sessions and for both genotypes there were no overall changes in the number of cells active per significant event (preplay vs replay, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, p>0.05, ranksum test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Across all experimental conditions and sessions and for both genotypes there were no overall changes in the duration of significant events.
source: in the duration of significant events (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, p>0.05, ranksum test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Across all experimental conditions and sessions and for both genotypes there were no overall changes in the extent of the linear track being represented during the significant events.
source: and in the extent of the linear track being represented during the significant events (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, p>0.05, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: For both genotypes and in all pre- and post-run sleep/rest sessions, the time of occurrence of significant preplay and replay events correlated with the time of occurrence of high-frequency oscillation ripples in the CA1.
source: For both genotypes and in all pre- and post-run sleep/rest sessions, the time of occurrence of significant preplay and replay events correlated with the time of occurrence of high-frequency oscillation ripples in the CA1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The experience- and CA3 NMDAR-dependent changes in replay over preplay described at the animal group level across sessions in the de novo condition was also found when the correlation values between place field templates and all spiking events were considered.
source: Interestingly, the experience- and CA3 NMDAR-dependent changes in replay over preplay described at the animal group level across sessions in the de novo condition was also found when the correlation values between place field templates and all spiking events (i.e., not only the significant ones) were considered (Figure 5Ca,b, solid bars).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5Ca,b.

claim: The correlation values of all spiking events during pre-DnRun1 sleep/rest exceeded the correlation values of all spiking events recorded during post-DnRun1 sleep/rest in CT but not KO mice.
source: The correlation values of all spiking events during pre-DnRun1 sleep/rest exceeded the correlation values of all spiking events recorded during post-DnRun1 sleep/rest in CT but not KO mice (p<10−5 in CT, p>0.5 in KO, Figure 5Ca, solid bars).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Ca.

claim: Preplay correlations were not different across genotypes.
source: Preplay correlations were not different across genotypes (p>0.9, ranksum test), but replay correlations were higher in the KO than CT mice (p<10−8, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Replay correlations were higher in the KO than CT mice.
source: Preplay correlations were not different across genotypes (p>0.9, ranksum test), but replay correlations were higher in the KO than CT mice (p<10−8, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: After a second experience on the novel track, the correlation values of all post-Run (replay) events became higher than the corresponding values of all pre-Run events in CT but not KO animals.
source: Moreover, after a second experience on the novel track (Figure 5Cb, solid bars), the correlation values of all post-Run (i.e., replay) events became higher than the corresponding values of all pre-Run events in CT (p<10−5) but not KO animals (p>0.5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5Cb.

claim: Despite the changes in correlation values from preplay to replay in CT mice, the proportions of significant events out of all of the detected events in all animals were similar in the pre-Run and post-Run sessions under all experimental conditions for both genotypes.
source: Despite the changes in correlation values from preplay to replay in CT mice, the proportions of significant events out of all of the detected events in all animals were similar in the pre-Run and post-Run sessions under all experimental conditions for both genotypes (Figure 5D, p>0.05, Z-test for two proportions).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The incidences of spiking events were similar in the sleep/rest sessions preceding and following the novel run experiences across conditions in both CT and KO mice.
source: The incidences of spiking events were similar in the sleep/rest sessions preceding and following the novel run experiences across conditions in both CT (p>0.08, paired t test) and KO mice (p>0.9).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Comparison of averages of absolute preplay and replay correlations over all experimental conditions and sessions performed altogether between the two genotypes revealed that correlation values were significantly higher in KO vs CT mice.
source: More importantly, comparison of averages of absolute preplay and replay correlations over all experimental conditions and sessions performed altogether between the two genotypes (eight sessions/genotype, paired by session type between genotypes) revealed that correlation values were significantly higher (p<0.006 for the significant correlations; p<0.009 for all the correlations; paired t test) and their variance was significantly lower (p<0.007, paired t test) in KO vs CT mice (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: The variance of correlation values was significantly lower in KO vs CT mice.
source: More importantly, comparison of averages of absolute preplay and replay correlations over all experimental conditions and sessions performed altogether between the two genotypes (eight sessions/genotype, paired by session type between genotypes) revealed that correlation values were significantly higher (p<0.006 for the significant correlations; p<0.009 for all the correlations; paired t test) and their variance was significantly lower (p<0.007, paired t test) in KO vs CT mice (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: The higher correlation values and lower variance in KO vs CT mice is consistent with the overall reduced experience-dependent changes in the correlation values in KO and indicates a reduced flexibility (increased rigidity) of the hippocampal network in the absence of NMDAR-dependent activity in the CA3 region.
source: This finding is consistent with the overall reduced experience-dependent changes in the correlation values in KO (Figures 4B,D,F,H and 5C) and indicates a reduced flexibility (increased rigidity) of the hippocampal network in the absence of NMDAR-dependent activity in the CA3 region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results comparing CT and KO mice.

claim: The overall spatial extent (proportion) of the linear track represented by the significant spiking events during sleep/rest was higher in the CT vs KO mice.
source: Moreover, the overall spatial extent (i.e., proportion) of the linear track represented by the significant spiking events during sleep/rest was higher in the CT vs KO mice (0.94 ± 0.01 compared to 0.89 ± 0.01 of the track length, p<0.027, paired t test), indicating a role for the NMDAR-dependent activity in the CA3 area in temporally linking together chunks of spatial sequences (Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006; Gupta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data and suggests a functional role for CA3 NMDARs.

claim: NMDAR-dependent activity in the CA3 area plays a role in temporally linking together chunks of spatial sequences.
source: Moreover, the overall spatial extent (i.e., proportion) of the linear track represented by the significant spiking events during sleep/rest was higher in the CT vs KO mice (0.94 ± 0.01 compared to 0.89 ± 0.01 of the track length, p<0.027, paired t test), indicating a role for the NMDAR-dependent activity in the CA3 area in temporally linking together chunks of spatial sequences (Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006; Gupta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results on spatial extent of sequences, drawing on cited literature.

claim: The differences in correlations between genotypes were not due to overall differences in the duration of the significant spiking events across genotypes.
source: These differences in correlations between genotypes were not due to overall differences in the duration of the significant spiking events (KO compared to CT across sessions, 0.33 ± 0.02 s compared to 0.33 ± 0.02 s, p=0.82, paired t test), or in the number of cells participating in these events (KO compared to CT, 6.1 ± 0.2 compared to 6.5 ± 0.2, p=0.65, paired t test) across genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The differences in correlations between genotypes were not due to overall differences in the number of cells participating in significant spiking events across genotypes.
source: These differences in correlations between genotypes were not due to overall differences in the duration of the significant spiking events (KO compared to CT across sessions, 0.33 ± 0.02 s compared to 0.33 ± 0.02 s, p=0.82, paired t test), or in the number of cells participating in these events (KO compared to CT, 6.1 ± 0.2 compared to 6.5 ± 0.2, p=0.65, paired t test) across genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Both groups of animals reached the criterion level of performance of 70% correct choices during the 10-day training on the delayed T-maze alternation task.
source: Both groups of animals reached the criterion level of performance of 70% correct choices during the 10-day training (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Analysis of the data from both genotypes during the 10-day training using a balanced two-way ANOVA test revealed a significant effect of the training day and genotype and a marginal duration (day) × genotype interaction.
source: Analysis of the data from both genotypes during the 10-day training using a balanced two-way ANOVA test (five blocks of 2 consecutive days) revealed a significant effect of the training day (F = 11.83, p=0.006) and genotype (F = 10.5, p=0.001) and a marginal duration (day) × genotype interaction (F = 3.24, p=0.057).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The KO subjects required additional sessions to reach the 70% criterion for learning to alternate compared to CT mice (9 vs 7 days).
source: Consistent with the difference in the neuronal dynamics across genotypes during the de novo condition (Figure 2A–D, left), the KO subjects required additional sessions to reach the 70% criterion for learning to alternate (9 vs 7 days, KO vs CT, Figure 6A; days 7–8 block, CT vs KO, 78.1% vs 53.7% correct, p=0.006, ranksum test) indicating the involvement of the intrinsic hippocampal circuitry in the acquisition of this task.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A and statistical analysis.

claim: The involvement of the intrinsic hippocampal circuitry in the acquisition of the alternation task is indicated by the difference in learning rate between CT and KO mice.
source: Consistent with the difference in the neuronal dynamics across genotypes during the de novo condition (Figure 2A–D, left), the KO subjects required additional sessions to reach the 70% criterion for learning to alternate (9 vs 7 days, KO vs CT, Figure 6A; days 7–8 block, CT vs KO, 78.1% vs 53.7% correct, p=0.006, ranksum test) indicating the involvement of the intrinsic hippocampal circuitry in the acquisition of this task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: The learning experience on the first T-maze greatly accelerated the acquisition of a similar alternation task in a second, novel T-maze configuration, when both groups of animals performed above threshold by the second day of re-training.
source: Moreover, consistent with the facilitation of neuronal dynamics on the novel arm by prior experience on the familiar track during the contiguous condition (Figure 2A–D, middle), this learning experience greatly accelerated (Tse et al., 2007) the acquisition of a similar alternation task in a second, novel T-maze configuration, when both groups of animals performed above threshold by the second day of re-training (Figure 6B, day 10 vs 12, 78.2% vs 77.6% correct, p=0.9 for CT, and 72.2% vs 75.7% correct, p=0.6 for KO, ranksum test).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B and statistical analysis.

claim: The behavioral results establish a correlation between the neuronal activity and the behavioral performances across genotypes and experimental conditions.
source: Together, these results establish a correlation between the neuronal activity and the behavioral performances across genotypes and experimental conditions and suggest that the dynamics of cell assembly organization are part of the underlying mechanisms of spatial learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined neuronal and behavioral results.

claim: The dynamics of cell assembly organization are part of the underlying mechanisms of spatial learning.
source: Together, these results establish a correlation between the neuronal activity and the behavioral performances across genotypes and experimental conditions and suggest that the dynamics of cell assembly organization are part of the underlying mechanisms of spatial learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined neuronal and behavioral results.

claim: A novel representation of a first-time experience on linear tracks (DnRun1) is formed in the CA1 area primarily on the framework of the preconfigured hippocampal network (preplay), which is modified, in part, during the experience and is rapidly stabilized primarily via CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity.
source: Our data have shown that a novel representation of a first-time experience on linear tracks (DnRun1) is formed in the CA1 area primarily on the framework of the preconfigured hippocampal network (preplay), which is modified, in part, during the experience and is rapidly stabilized primarily via CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the main findings.

claim: The changes in place cell activity occur without affecting the general stability of the hippocampal network, which indicates a homeostatic regulation of its temporal sequence activity in response to novelty.
source: The changes in place cell activity occur without affecting the general stability of the hippocampal network, which indicates a homeostatic regulation of its temporal sequence activity in response to novelty: ∼10% of the temporal sequences reflect the novel experience during the subsequent sleep/rest period, a proportion that is not different from the proportion of corresponding preplay events.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results on the stability of event proportions.

claim: Approximately 10% of the temporal sequences reflect the novel experience during the subsequent sleep/rest period, a proportion that is not different from the proportion of corresponding preplay events.
source: The changes in place cell activity occur without affecting the general stability of the hippocampal network, which indicates a homeostatic regulation of its temporal sequence activity in response to novelty: ∼10% of the temporal sequences reflect the novel experience during the subsequent sleep/rest period, a proportion that is not different from the proportion of corresponding preplay events.
evidence: This is supported by the data on event proportions.

claim: Subsequent exposures to the same track (DnRun2) and additional contiguous (ContigRun) or isolated novel tracks (DisjRun1) resulted in the expression of similar proportions of correlated temporal sequences before and after the corresponding novel spatial experiences, both in control and CA3 NMDAR KO mice.
source: Subsequent exposures to the same track (DnRun2) and additional contiguous (ContigRun) or isolated novel tracks (DisjRun1) resulted in the expression of similar proportions of correlated temporal sequences before and after the corresponding novel spatial experiences, both in control and CA3 NMDAR KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by the data on event proportions across conditions.

claim: The overall robust homeostasis of the hippocampal network seen at the temporal sequence level and expressed during offline states of sleep and rest reflects the default sequential cell assembly architecture of the hippocampal network shaped by the multiple unaccounted experiences the animal has had in the past.
source: We propose that the overall robust homeostasis of the hippocampal network seen at the temporal sequence level and expressed during offline states of sleep and rest reflects the default sequential cell assembly architecture of the hippocampal network shaped by the multiple unaccounted experiences the animal has had in the past.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results.

claim: The proposal that the hippocampal network homeostasis reflects default sequential cell assembly architecture is consistent with previous studies reporting that temporal sequences emitted during onsite resting periods do not specifically reflect the recent spatial experience of the animal.
source: Our proposal is consistent with previous studies reporting that temporal sequences emitted during onsite resting periods do not specifically reflect the recent spatial experience of the animal (Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Gupta et al., 2010; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013), but rather reflect multiple related spatial experiences the animal had experienced or will experience in the near future in that particular environment (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by cited literature.

claim: The overall stability of the hippocampal network during sleep/rest epochs on both sides of the novel spatial experiences does not mean that the novel experiences did not induce more discrete plastic changes which are apparent at the individual cell level in the network.
source: The overall stability of the hippocampal network during sleep/rest epochs on both sides of the novel spatial experiences does not mean that the novel experiences did not induce more discrete plastic changes which are apparent at the individual cell level in the network (Dragoi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results, drawing on cited literature.

claim: In the absence of CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity, the CA1 temporal firing sequences appear more rigid and their correlations with the place cell sequences are less modulated by the recent experiences compared to control animals.
source: More importantly, in the absence of CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity, the CA1 temporal firing sequences appear more rigid and their correlations with the place cell sequences are less modulated by the recent experiences compared to control animals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results comparing CT and KO mice.

claim: In the absence of CA3 NMDARs, the CA1 cellular assemblies are less affected by the animals' novel spatial experiences and maintain an increased correlation across different brain states, behaviors, and experiences.
source: Overall, in the absence of CA3 NMDARs, the event correlations with future place cell sequences exhibit lower variance and higher values than in the presence of CA3 NMDARs. These results indicate that the organization of cellular assemblies in the CA1 area is influenced by the NMDAR-dependent activity in the upstream CA3 area. In the absence of this type of activity/plasticity, the CA1 cellular assemblies are less affected by the animals' novel spatial experiences and maintain an increased correlation across different brain states (i.e., across sharp-wave/ripples during sleep and theta during run), behaviors, and experiences.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results comparing CT and KO mice.

claim: The reduced flexibility of CA1 cellular assemblies in the absence of CA3 NMDARs could explain why the mutant animals exhibit deficits in one trial learning which involves rapid plastic changes in hippocampal cellular assemblies.
source: This could explain why the mutant animals exhibit deficits in one trial learning which involves rapid plastic changes in hippocampal cellular assemblies (Nakazawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results, drawing on cited literature.

claim: A hallmark of neurons' organization in cellular assemblies is their onsite coordinated activation across similar animal behaviors such as running laps.
source: A hallmark of neurons' organization in cellular assemblies is their onsite coordinated activation across similar animal behaviors such as running laps (Wills et al., 2005; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Upon familiarization with a novel linear track, the lap-by-lap correlations between place cell pairs increase rapidly during the exploratory session in control animals but remain low for several exploratory sessions in the absence of CA3 NMDARs.
source: Here we show that upon familiarization with a novel linear track, the lap-by-lap correlations between place cell pairs increase rapidly during the exploratory session in control animals but remain low for several exploratory sessions in the absence of CA3 NMDARs.
evidence: This is a summary of the results on lap-by-lap correlations.

claim: NMDAR-dependent activity within the CA3 area of the hippocampus is involved in the rapid organization and linking of CA1 place cells in cellular assemblies during the encoding of a first-time and of subsequent isolated novel experiences on linear tracks.
source: These results suggest that NMDAR-dependent activity within the CA3 area of the hippocampus is involved in the rapid organization and linking of CA1 place cells in cellular assemblies during the encoding of a first-time and of subsequent isolated novel experiences on linear tracks, but is not necessary for the general expression of temporal sequences of place cells in the CA1 in the form of preplay and replay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results comparing CT and KO mice.

claim: NMDAR-dependent activity within the CA3 area is not necessary for the general expression of temporal sequences of place cells in the CA1 in the form of preplay and replay.
source: These results suggest that NMDAR-dependent activity within the CA3 area of the hippocampus is involved in the rapid organization and linking of CA1 place cells in cellular assemblies during the encoding of a first-time and of subsequent isolated novel experiences on linear tracks, but is not necessary for the general expression of temporal sequences of place cells in the CA1 in the form of preplay and replay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results showing similar event proportions in CT and KO mice.

claim: Quite often, a single exposure to absolutely novel experiences does not lead to a lasting memory of the experience, whereas repeated exposures to the same experience or prior knowledge with similar kind of experiences result in more rapid learning and memory consolidation.
source: Quite often, a single exposure to absolutely novel experiences does not lead to a lasting memory of the experience, whereas repeated exposures to the same experience or prior knowledge with similar kind of experiences result in more rapid learning and memory consolidation (Tse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The increased map stability, tuning, and cell assembly co-variation found in repeatedly exposed and in experienced, but not in naïve animals underlie the rapid consolidation of episodic memories of repeated or related new experiences, but not of entirely novel ones.
source: We propose that the increased map stability, tuning, and cell assembly co-variation we find in repeatedly exposed and in experienced, but not in naïve animals underlie the rapid consolidation of episodic memories of repeated or related new experiences, but not of entirely novel ones.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results.

claim: Entirely novel experiences may require repeated exposure to engage hippocampal replay-dependent mechanisms for memory consolidation.
source: The latter may instead require repeated exposure to engage hippocampal replay-dependent mechanisms for memory consolidation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The intact hippocampus is essential for encoding and rapid consolidation of memory.
source: The intact hippocampus is essential for encoding and rapid consolidation of memory (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1992; Eichenbaum et al., 1999) and for associative-novelty detection (Kumaran and Maguire, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The intact hippocampus is essential for associative-novelty detection.
source: The intact hippocampus is essential for encoding and rapid consolidation of memory (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1992; Eichenbaum et al., 1999) and for associative-novelty detection (Kumaran and Maguire, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The role of the hippocampus and of NMDA receptors in learning and memory consolidation is manifested primarily in experimentally naïve animals and diminishes with experience.
source: The role of the hippocampus and of NMDA receptors in learning and memory consolidation is manifested primarily in experimentally naïve animals and diminishes with experience (Bannerman et al., 1995; Otnaess et al., 1999), when new information is presumably rapidly integrated into pre-existing neocortical frameworks of knowledge, or schemas (Morris, 2006; Tse et al., 2007; McKenzie and Eichenbaum, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: When new information is rapidly integrated into pre-existing neocortical frameworks of knowledge, or schemas, the role of the hippocampus and NMDA receptors diminishes with experience.
source: The role of the hippocampus and of NMDA receptors in learning and memory consolidation is manifested primarily in experimentally naïve animals and diminishes with experience (Bannerman et al., 1995; Otnaess et al., 1999), when new information is presumably rapidly integrated into pre-existing neocortical frameworks of knowledge, or schemas (Morris, 2006; Tse et al., 2007; McKenzie and Eichenbaum, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The neural substrates of schema-based learning and memory processes are believed to be the formation of stable, finely tuned cellular assemblies across the neocortex and the hippocampus.
source: The neural substrates of such learning and memory processes are believed to be the formation of stable, finely tuned cellular assemblies (Hebb, 1949) across the neocortex and the hippocampus (Tse et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: In addition to changes in the activity of individual CA1 neurons, their ability to rapidly and flexibly organize in stable cellular assemblies underlies the process of learning and memory.
source: We propose that, in addition to changes in the activity of individual CA1 neurons, their ability to rapidly and flexibly organize in stable cellular assemblies underlies the process of learning and memory.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results.

claim: Familiarization with the spatial environment and the behavioral task are associated with the formation of cortical mental schemas that rely on the stability of neocortical-hippocampal cellular assemblies.
source: Familiarization with the spatial environment and the behavioral task are associated with the formation of cortical mental schemas (Tse et al., 2007; McKenzie et al., 2013) that rely on the stability of neocortical-hippocampal cellular assemblies.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation drawing on cited literature.

claim: Stable neocortical-hippocampal cellular assemblies function like strong neural attractors that will integrate future neuronal representations.
source: These function like strong neural attractors (Tsodyks, 1999; Wills et al., 2005) that will integrate future neuronal representations.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation drawing on cited literature.

claim: The group of CA1 place cell pairs that maintained high levels of lap-by-lap co-variation and preserved the relative distance between their place fields across different environments independent of CA3 NMDARs (stable assemblies) may represent one neuronal mechanism underlying schema-based accelerated learning.
source: The group of CA1 place cell pairs that maintained high levels of lap-by-lap co-variation and preserved the relative distance between their place fields across different environments independent of CA3 NMDARs (stable assemblies, disjunct condition; contiguous condition) may represent one neuronal mechanism underlying schema-based accelerated learning.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results on stable assemblies.

claim: Lesion experiments have argued for a transient, but necessary role of the intact hippocampus in the assimilation and consolidation of new information into schemas.
source: Previously, lesion experiments have argued for a transient, but necessary role of the intact hippocampus in the assimilation and consolidation of new information into schemas (Tse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity and synaptic plasticity are not necessary for either the rapid assimilation of new contiguous locations into a previously established spatial representation or for learning of a related alternation task.
source: Whereas not speaking for the whole hippocampus, our data indicate that CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity and synaptic plasticity are not necessary for either the rapid assimilation of new contiguous locations into a previously established spatial representation or for learning of a related alternation task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from the contiguous condition and T-maze 2.

claim: CA3 NMDAR-dependent activity and synaptic plasticity are necessary for the rapid formation of new CA1 cell assemblies in the hippocampus of experimentally naïve animals and the development of a new schema associated with the first-time learning of a hippocampal-dependent alternation task.
source: Instead, this type of plasticity is necessary for the rapid formation of new CA1 cell assemblies in the hippocampus of experimentally naïve animals and the development of a new schema associated with the first-time learning of a hippocampal-dependent alternation task (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from the de novo condition and T-maze 1.

claim: The existence of a mechanistic dichotomy between different forms of learning may help explain why hippocampal dysfunction results in anterograde amnesia while recollection of old, schema-based memories is preserved.
source: The existence of a mechanistic dichotomy between these different forms of learning may help explain why hippocampal dysfunction results in anterograde amnesia (Scoville and Milner, 1957) while recollection of old, schema-based memories (Winocur et al., 2005) is preserved.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results, drawing on cited literature.
